key_insight: For CBCT-based TMJ osteoarthritis detection, the biggest performance gain came from partially unfreezing the last two transformer blocks of a DINO-style vision transformer, not from changing the backbone alone.
clinical_relevance: This suggests self-supervised foundation models can be effectively adapted for low-data dental imaging tasks, potentially improving automated screening of subtle TMJ OA changes on CBCT.
method: Axial CBCT slices were encoded with DINO-family ViT backbones and combined with attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL).
Compared frozen versus partially adapted backbones across DINOv1, DINOv2, DINOv2+reg, RAD-DINO, and a supervised ImageNet ViT-B/16 baseline.
Ablation tested different unfreezing and aggregation strategies for patient-level binary OA vs normal classification.
evidence_signal: On a multi-source CBCT dataset, partial unfreezing of the final two transformer blocks improved AUC from 0.671 (fully frozen DINOv2) to 0.902, outperforming DINOv1 (0.867), DINOv2+reg (0.774), and supervised ViT-B/16 (0.843).
watch_item: The findings are based on a specific multi-source CBCT setup, so performance may vary with scanner protocols, cohort mix, and external validation settings.
paper_title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers for CBCT-Based Detection of Temporomandibular Joint Osteoarthritis
